analysis.one_liner: Lets the Postal Service offer low-fee checking, savings, and small loans, bypassing banks and payday lenders.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 19, 2024 with one cosponsor and died in committee two weeks later when the Congress ended, with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let the U.S. Postal Service offer basic banking at its post offices: small checking and savings accounts, debit cards, check cashing, bill pay, money transfers, and small loans of up to $500. Loan interest and fees would be capped at essentially the federal government's own borrowing rate, and savings accounts would pay at least the national average bank rate. The Postal Service would have to provide these services itself, not through partnerships with private banks. The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households without bank accounts and households that rely on payday loans, check cashers, and overdraft fees would gain an affordable alternative available at thousands of post offices, including in rural areas and neighborhoods banks have left. The roughly 4 to 6 million unbanked American households targeted by the bill's funding provision would save on fees and borrowing costs.

how_it_helps.text: The Postal Service could offer small-dollar loans of up to $500 at a time, or up to $1,000 within a year of a first loan, with total interest and fees capped at 101 percent of the one-month Treasury rate — a tiny fraction of typical payday-loan costs.
It could offer small checking and savings accounts of up to $20,000 per account, plus debit cards, check cashing, automatic bill pay, mobile banking, and domestic and international money transfers.
Savings accounts would have to pay interest at least equal to 100 percent of the FDIC's weekly national rate on non-jumbo savings accounts.
Services must be offered by the Postal Service itself, exclusively, and not through a partnership or contract with private financial institutions, keeping the public option direct and low-cost.

The Federal Reserve would transfer to the Postmaster General sums sufficient to substantially decrease the number of people without bank accounts or using payday lending, check cashing, prepaid debit cards, and overdraft fees.
The Comptroller General would report annually to Congress on who uses the services, their demographics, and how the products are used, creating built-in oversight.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders, check-cashing services, and prepaid debit card providers would lose the fee and interest income they earn from customers the Postal Service would serve. Banks and credit unions would forgo some fee income and low-cost deposits, though the bill forbids the Postal Service from becoming a chartered, insured bank. If the program lost money, the Federal Reserve funding mechanism could ultimately spread costs beyond postal revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders, check cashers, and banks

drawbacks.text: The Postal Service is already under severe financial strain, and a loan cap set at roughly the government's own borrowing rate is far below what small-dollar loans typically cost to make; critics argue the program could require ongoing public subsidy rather than paying for itself.

The bill funds the program through transfers from the Federal Reserve, an unusual arrangement that draws the central bank into funding a postal lending operation and would likely face strong objections from the Fed and the banking industry.

By barring any partnership with private banks, the bill forecloses middle-ground designs (like partnering with community banks or credit unions) that some reformers have proposed as cheaper to launch.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of households who today pay triple-digit annual rates for small loans and heavy fees for cashing checks, the bill offers a concrete, large benefit: a public alternative at post-office counters, with near-zero loan rates and full-fee disclosure built into the cap. The real risks are on the sustainability side — a capped-rate loan book run by an agency that is already losing money could need the open-ended Federal Reserve funding the bill authorizes, and the bill was introduced so late in the session that no committee work examined those questions. The honest weighing: potentially large gains for unbanked households, with a genuine open question about who absorbs the program's operating losses.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final two weeks of the Congress and referred to the Senate Homeland Security committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 19, 2024, by Senator Gillibrand together with Senator Sanders.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
No further action — no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote — was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders, check-cashing and prepaid card businesses, and banks that earn fees from unbanked and underbanked customers are better off, because the competing public alternative never advanced. The Postal Service is no worse off, since it was never required to build the program.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Postal Banking Act on December 19, 2024.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill with Gillibrand, the bill's sole cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 19, 2024 and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators were ever attached to the bill — one Democrat and one Independent — and no member publicly opposed it in the record, so no partisan split was ever tested.

industries.note: The Postal Service would directly compete for their core customers with loans capped near the Treasury rate and low-fee check cashing. Their business model of high-fee small-dollar lending to unbanked households is what the bill's funding provision explicitly aims to decrease.

Postal accounts would draw away fee income and low-cost deposits, though the bill caps the exposure by forbidding the Postal Service from obtaining a bank charter or becoming an insured depository institution, and forbids partnerships with private institutions.

The bill would add financial services to the Postal Service's statutory mission and create a dedicated Federal Reserve funding stream for it, making USPS the permanent public channel for small-dollar banking. For customers, this is the benefit itself; for the agency, it is a major new mandate.
